meta.title: Who really said "Firearms stand next in importance to the Constitution itself. They are the American people's liberty teeth and keystone under independence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — George Washington never said it. The line was written by gun writer C. S. Wheatley in a 1926 magazine and later misattributed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Firearms stand next in importance to the Constitution itself. They are the American people's liberty teeth and keystone under independence'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Washington. Quote Investigator traced the wording to C. S. Wheatley’s own 1926 commentary in Hunter-Trader-Trapper magazine.

answer.label: Not George Washington — written by C. S. Wheatley in 1926
answer.sourceLine: George Washington never wrote or spoke these words. Quote Investigator traced the passage to an outdoor-sports writer, C. S. Wheatley, whose September 1926 opinion piece “Older Ideas of Firearms” in Hunter-Trader-Trapper magazine ran the line as his own commentary — unquoted — right after a sentence that mentioned a Washington address. Later readers mistook Wheatley’s words for Washington’s, and the misattribution spread through newspapers in the 1970s–80s.

author.name: C. S. Wheatley
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: C. S. Wheatley was a contributor to Hunter-Trader-Trapper, a Columbus, Ohio periodical for hunters and trappers. Almost nothing is recorded about him beyond the September 1926 article “Older Ideas of Firearms,” in which the “liberty teeth” sentence appears as his own editorializing — not as a quotation of anyone. The thought is his; the famous attribution to George Washington is a reading error that took hold decades later.

misattribution.heading: How it went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely circulated fake “Founder” gun quotes. The wording is real — but it belongs to a 1926 magazine writer, not to George Washington.

items.why: The line appears in none of Washington’s writings, letters, or speeches. Mount Vernon’s estate lists it among spurious quotations: “This quotation does not show up in any of Washington’s writings, nor does any closely related quote.”

Quote Investigator found the passage in Wheatley’s September 1926 article in Hunter-Trader-Trapper, written as his own opinion; the sentence just before it referenced a Washington address, which seeded the confusion.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is C. S. Wheatley’s 1926 editorial opinion, misattributed to Washington by readers who mistook adjacent sentences — documented by Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why this one keeps circulating
lead: The sentence has become a fixture of gun-rights memes and speeches precisely because it sounds like an 18th-century founder: terse, aphoristic, constitutional. But its earliest trace is a 1926 hobbyist magazine, and the passage carries tells that betray a modern hand — references and phrasing (“prairie wagon,” a “99 99/100 percent” statistic) that don’t fit Washington’s era or diction.

The misattribution is a textbook case of a quotation-mark error: Wheatley named a Washington address in one sentence, then gave his own opinion in the next without quotation marks, and later copyists collapsed the two.
context.pull: The thought was a 1926 gun writer’s — Washington’s name was pinned on it decades later.
